title: Same Base Model. Different Methods. Different Trade-offs.
Same Base Model.
Different Methods.
Different Trade-offs.

intro.before: You rarely need to update every weight. Which parameters you train decides
intro.after: , so pick the lightest method that reaches your target.

bullets.text: Trains all weights: maximum flexibility
Best fit for large domain shifts
No extra modules at inference time
Needs memory for grads and optimizer state
Freezes W, trains small matrices A and B
Trains a tiny fraction of the weights
Merge BA into W: no added latency
Low rank can limit big behaviour changes
Base frozen in 4-bit NF4, adapters in 16-bit
Fits larger models on a single GPU
Paged optimizers absorb memory spikes
Slower steps: weights dequantize on the fly
Adds bottleneck layers, base stays frozen
Swap one adapter per task on a shared base
Well studied, many variants
Extra layers add some inference latency
Learns prefix vectors for every layer
Tiny share of params; weights unchanged
One small prefix file per task
Uses context length; can be unstable to train

items.title: Prompt Tuning
items.tagline: Learn the prompt, not the model

bullets.text: Learns a few soft-prompt vectors at the input
Smallest footprint: kilobytes per task
Closes the gap on very large models
Weaker than LoRA on smaller models

principles.sub: Try parameter-efficient methods first; full fine-tuning needs far more memory and data.
High-quality, on-task examples matter more than which adapter you pick.
Check general skills too; narrow data can degrade abilities you still need.

rows.q: Big domain shift, lots of data

quote.big: Train fewer weights, ship more models.
quote.small: Pick the lightest method that hits the bar.
